newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMANY'S STOIBER BEATS DRUM AGAIN FOR EMU DELAY.
newsitem.headline: GERMANY'S STOIBER BEATS DRUM AGAIN FOR EMU DELAY.

text.p: Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber, ending a truce with Chancellor Helmut Kohl in a dispute over Europe's planned single currency, on Thursday stepped up his campaign to delay the launch of economic and monetary union.
Kohl, following days of scathing criticism of monetary union by Stoiber, caved in last month to the pressure and made clear that Germany would not accept a soft European currency.

But Stoiber appears to have ended a six week old peace with Kohl and this week launched a new round of attacks in interviews with international newspapers aimed at floating an alternative to launching monetary union on time in 1999.

While not ruling out a punctual launch of the new euro currency, Stoiber insists that Germany and France, the twin engines of European integration, both strictly meet the fiscal targets this year to qualify for monetary union.
"If France or Germany do not respect the criteria to the letter we will find another alternative," Stoiber said in an interview with financial daily La Tribune on Thursday.

"I can easily imagine that the best solution is to give ourselves two extra years, until 1999, to meet the criteria and then reduce the intermediate phase," said Stoiber, a member of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union party.

Stoiber warned that the current weakness of the mark, in part a reflection of market concerns about a soft euro, could spark a political backlash in Germany if people see their hard-earned savings eroded away by inflation and a weak euro.
Should the mark continue to slide against the dollar and major European currencies, Stoiber warned that the powerful Bundesbank could step in and raise interest rates.
"If the dollar was to climb over two marks, it is difficult to see how the Bundesbank could not react, with all the negative consequences for Europe," Stoiber said.
Should the Bundesbank raise official interest rates, other European countries would be forced to follow suit, threatening the moderate recovery in most economies on the continent.
"Better to avoid reaching that point," Stoiber added.

The Bavarian premiere, branded a Eurosceptic by Kohl's camp who see Stoiber's intiatives as unwanted interference, made similar comments this week in an interview with Dutch newspaper Algemeen Dagblad and in the German daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung.

Stoiber's office in Munich explained that he has worked out a proposal, that has been discussed with Waigel, that would delay the planned fixing of European exchange rates but not the final phase of monetary union.
European exchange rate parities are due to be fixed on January 1, 1999, with euro bills and coins coming into circulation in 2002.

Stoiber suggested that European countries did not need three years to put the euro into operation and that by fixing exchange rates on January 1, 2001, instead of in 1999, Europe could still introduce the new currency on time in 2002.

Independent economists have long considered this the most likely scenario should Germany and France overshoot the goal of limiting budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product as called for in the Maastricht Treaty.
Such a plan would give European Union members more time to meet the Maastricht targets without delaying the final conversion to a single currency.

"This version bears the credibility of the entire project and would give candidates two extra years to qualify for monetary union honestly and with undeniable marks," said the Sueddeutsch Zeitung in an editorial backing Stoiber.
The paper also chided Kohl for continuing to insist that Germany would meet the monetary union targets this year when all evidence pointed to the contrary.
"This promise is cynical with respect to intelligent citizens who know that it cannot be kept, at least not honestly," the paper said.

The respected Ifo economic research institute said last week that Germany's budget deficit would reach 3.3 percent GDP in 1997, but that this should not prevent Bonn from qualifying for monetary union.
